When deployed, we receive lots of care packages. Candy is popular, and toiletries for some reason. Also tracts, Bibles, and flyers from every denomination that supports the military. The candy is usually appreciated, we're required to pack enough toiletries to cover the trip so those are almost useless (unless there's an accident with the baggage, you ever seen a shoe full of shampoo?), and religious materials are kind of uncomfortable to throw away. The big thing about all of these is we already have them there, and with enough selection to find the one you want. Amazon delivers to APO, so the weird stuff we need can be had in a week.

The game over there is "hurry up and wait," so things that have been really great to get by surprise:

  • Games. I've played a fair amount of chess over there, and never had a decent chess set. There's always a checker with a K on it or a dice for a pawn. Farkle was big last time I was there, and I only recently found out there's little travel ones that are easier to keep in a pocket.

  • Puzzles. The metal or wooden ones that you have to figure out how to take apart and put back together. I wore the stickers off a Rubik's cube on a deployment a couple years ago. Word search and Sudoku also are greatly loved.

  • Books. Good books, new books, old books. Familiar titles, books that are becoming movies soon.

If you want to make up care packages there's lots of ways to find out how to address them, or I can help. If you know someone who will deploy soon, keep in touch and once you're sure the mail service is working wherever they are, send a gift card around the first quarter to third of the trip. This is the time one really realizes what's missing and there's plenty of time for the package to arrive and be enjoyed for the majority of the stay.

Another good way to support a troop during deployment is helping the family with chores. My wife can't mow the yard when I'm gone, and a good friend is always welcome to help out. That's the kind of thing we need.

I'm on Firefox, so all this is for Firefox.

  • AdBlock Plus - uBlock supposedly uses less RAM, but I use Firefox so it's already clear that I don't give a shit about that. There's been drama and like 3 different forks with uBlock, so I might switch over in a few months after it's all been quiet for a while.
  • BetterTTV - I stream and watch things on Twitch.tv, and this improves Twitch.tv, especially the chat.
  • Bookmarks Checker - Automated checker to go through your bookmarks and see which ones throw up error codes, so that you can clean up your bookmarks. I've been transferring my bookmarks over through reformats and new computers for at least 8 years now, so this is a god-send.
  • Classic Theme Restorer - Want Firefox to look like Firefox again, instead of Chrome? This adds back in many of the options that were removed in the controversial Australis UI change.
  • Ghostery - Stop scripts that track you on the internet. This isn't any of that NoScript stuff, where it keeps you safe at the expense of you basically having to whitelist half the damn internet just to do your daily browsing. This is incredibly easy to customize, and blocks very little that actually interferes with using websites.
  • Google Search by Image - This is actually linked to by Google. It allows you to right click->Search Image on Google to find the source of an image, or similar images.
  • Greasemonkey - This just gives you the ability to run scripts. Mostly, I use it for 4chan-x.
  • HTTPS-Everywhere - Made by the EFF. Automatically makes many popular sites use HTTPS, which is more secure and private than HTTP, whenever it's available.
  • ReloadEvery - Ever had a website you had to F5 a bunch on? Automate it.
  • TinEye Reverse Image Search - Same idea as Google Search by Image, but uses TinEye instead of Google. It helps you find the source of an image.
  • YesScript - NoScript blacklists everything by default, and you have to whitelist the bits you want to enable. This is the opposite. Everything works by default, but you can blacklist those pesky scripts that you encounter.

If you get AdBlock Plus, here are the subscriptions I subscribe to:

  • EasyList and EasyPrivacy - The main ABP filter, with extra stuff to block tracking scripts that collect your personal data.
  • Malware Domain Blocklist - Kinda self-explanatory.
  • Prebake - Gets rid of those "HI I AM A WEBSITE I LIKE COOKIES" notices.
  • Spam404 - Blocks spam domains.
  • Anti-Adblock Killer - Block messages that scold you for using adblockers. So meta.

Here are my installed addons in no particular order:

  • Blender - spoofs your user agent to the most common. eg. Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 6.3; WOW64; rv:36.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/36.0
  • Cookie Whitelist - Only allows cookies from whitelisted sites, can temporarily approve cookies which are deleted when my browser is restarted.
  • DownThemAll! - Awesome download manager / accelerator / bulk downloader. I use it most often to download manga since I can download and sort hundreds of pages in seconds.
  • Ghostery - Blocks blacklisted trackers. uBlock has the same functionality, but is a little less user friendly.
  • uBlock - The latest and greatest ad-blocker. So slick that Adblock Edge, another excellent blocker, was actually discontinued because uBlock is better in every way.
  • HTTPS Everywhere - Automatically forces encrypted connections to all sites that support HTTPS.
  • NoScript - A classic and absolute MUST have. Acts like a virtual condom against a plethora of virtual STDs. You can't even realize just how much crap is out there until you install this and it borks half the web.
  • Thumbnail Zoom Plus - Eh, kinda works, hover over a thumbnail or image link to have it displayed at full size in a temporary window. Great for browsing dank memes.
  • WOT (Web Of Trust) - Website reputation and review service. Take ratings with a grain of salt, it's most useful for clearly flagging malicious, or undesirable sites when sifting through search engine results.

Most of my addons are security oriented. Using this combination I've managed to stay pretty safe even in those moments where common sense has eluded me :p

The Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FFDCA) grants FDA authority to ensure the safety of all domestic and imported foods. The FFDCA requires pre-market safety testing of any food additive (defined as a substance intentionally added to food) unless a decision is made that the additive is Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS). GRAS substances do not require testing of any kind. A 1992 Statement of Policy promulgated by FDA argues that genes added to common food substances via genetic engineering are GRAS because the new food is largely the same as its conventional counterpart. The preponderant majority of experts on the FDA’s Biotechnology Task Force has concluded that GE foods pose unusual risks and cannot be presumed safe.
